Tutors
TYOO-torz
n. pl. (guardians having charge of a minor heir)
Greek epitropos, a steward or guardian — one entrusted with the care of a person or estate. Latin tutor, a protector or guardian, from tueri, to watch over. The legal sense is primary: not a teacher, but the custodian of a child heir.

Biblical Definition

But is under tutors and governors until the time appointed of the father. Paul is making a legal argument and the vocabulary is technical. Under Roman practice an heir who was still a minor was placed under guardians and stewards; he owned the whole estate in principle and controlled none of it in practice, and the arrangement ended on a date the father had fixed. Paul says so in the preceding verse: the heir, as long as he is a child, differeth nothing from a servant, though he be lord of all. That is his picture of the covenant people under the law — genuine heirs, under genuine tutelage, waiting on a date they did not set. The application follows: even so we, when we were children, were in bondage under the elements of the world. And then the hinge of the whole passage turns on that appointed date, which arrived exactly when the Father had determined, to redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons. Two things follow for the reading of the Old Testament. The law was not a mistake or a rival system; a guardian is appointed by the father and acts with his authority, which is why Paul calls the law holy, and just, and good. And the guardianship was always temporary by design, terminating not at the heir's initiative but at the father's appointed time.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): a guardian; one who has the charge of a child or pupil and his estate; one who instructs.

expand to see more

TUTOR, n. A guardian; one who has the charge of a child or pupil and his estate.

TUTOR, n. An instructor; one who has the care of instructing another in various branches of learning.

GOVERNOR, n. One who governs; one invested with supreme authority; a tutor; one who has the care of a young man.

GUARDIAN, n. One who has the care of an orphan or minor, and of his estate, by legal appointment.

HEIR, n. The man who succeeds or is to succeed another in the possession of property.

Key Scripture

Galatians 4:2 — "But is under tutors and governors until the time appointed of the father."

Galatians 4:1 — "Now I say, That the heir, as long as he is a child, differeth nothing from a servant, though he be lord of all;"

Galatians 4:3 — "Even so we, when we were children, were in bondage under the elements of the world:"

Galatians 4:5 — "To redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons."

Modern Corruption

The law is treated either as a discarded system belonging to a superseded people or as still binding in its ceremonial administration; Paul makes it a guardianship appointed by the Father and ended at his appointed time.

expand to see more

Antinomian readings take Galatians 4 as proof that the law has simply been abolished, and with it any continuing rule for the Christian life. The image will not carry it. A tutor appointed by the father is not an enemy, and the ending of a guardianship does not mean the guardian was wrong. Paul says elsewhere that the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good, and that faith does not make it void but establishes it. What ended was the covenant administration under which the heir was kept as a servant; what remains is the moral law, written now in the heart under the new covenant.

The opposite error keeps the guardianship running past its term. Wherever Christians are placed under ceremonial requirements — dietary law, festival calendars, circumcision, or their functional equivalents in later church tradition — the minor is being returned to the nursery after the father has declared him of age. That was precisely the Galatian error, and Paul's response to it is the sharpest language in his letters. The doctrine at stake is adoption: the point of the passage is that the appointed time came, the Son was sent, and the heirs received the standing of sons. To go back under tutors is to deny that the date arrived.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek epitropos (G2012), a guardian or steward; oikonomos (G3623), a house-manager; prothesmia (G4287), an appointed time; huiothesia (G5206), adoption of sons.

expand to see more

Greek epitropos (G2012) — a guardian entrusted with a minor; rendered tutors.

Greek oikonomos (G3623) — a steward of an estate; rendered governors.

Greek prothesmia (G4287) — a time appointed beforehand; its only occurrence, and the hinge of the argument.

Greek huiothesia (G5206) — the placing as a son, adoption; what the appointed time brought.

Greek paidagogos (G3807) — a child-conductor; rendered schoolmaster in the parallel at Galatians 3:24.

Usage

"“under tutors and governors” — a legal guardianship, not schooling."

"“until the time appointed of the father” — a date the heir did not set."

"“that we might receive the adoption of sons” — what the date brought."
